03 — Dashboard Insights

What the data told us.

Finding 01

The 20.7-day lag is the root cause

Every wrong citation traces to one decision: updating data once a night. 20.7 days average delay between permit issuance and officer visibility.

Finding 02

51.7% manual entry = 51.7% risk

Over half the database is entered by hand. 517 of 1,000 records are at risk of transcription error before reaching the batch upload.

Finding 03

300 wrong citations — system failure

Officers were doing their jobs correctly. 30% of all citations were issued against valid permits using stale data.

Finding 04

Zone Z5 is the critical hotspot

Most records (220), most errors (71), most manual entries (115). Zone Z5 is where the fix would have the fastest visible impact.

Finding 05

$40,386 is the measurable cost

Fines the city issued and then waived because citations were wrong. 37% of $108,705 total fines — lost to bad data.

Finding 06

3 systems, 0 shared truth

Enforcement (345), Permit (331), Finance (324) each hold their own records. No master database means every discrepancy is a potential error.

Operations

Data lag by permit type

Visitor: 21.2 days · Commercial: 20.7 days · Residential: 20.2 days. No permit type escapes the batch delay.

Operations

Citation error rate by type

Visitor permits: 31.7% · Residential: 29.8% · Commercial: 28.4%. Visitor permits — most frequently renewed — suffer the most.

Operations

Permit status split

Active: 351 (35.1%) · Suspended: 328 (32.8%) · Expired: 321 (32.1%). 64.9% of permits are not active.

Revenue Breakdown — Dataset 1

Finance

$33,672 collected

Only 31% of total fines issued have been paid. The rest is pending or lost.

06 — Conclusion

One root cause. One fix.

From fragmented to unified.

Riverton's parking operations suffer from one architectural decision — a nightly batch process that keeps departments 20 days apart. The proposed centralized system eliminates that gap, and with it, nearly every downstream problem.
